transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-10 15:00 PST
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Samantha Lee (Redwood AE), Diego Martinez (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (HorizonLedger CTO), Marcus Holt (Lead Backend), Elena Park (Security), Ryan Cho (Product)

Summary: quick hosted API handoff + live mini demo focusing on streaming behavior, parameter knobs (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), and retry/playback patterns; discussed security constraints (KMS, retention), pilot scope, benchmarks.

00:00 Samantha: hey everyone thanks for joining — quick round of intros then we'll jump into a tiny live demo and then the retry/playbook.
00:11 Priya: hi all Priya here, CTO at HorizonLedger, we mainly want to understand latency patterns and how retries affect cost.
00:18 Marcus: Marcus — backend, we care about idempotency and how to avoid duplicate messages when we retry.
00:24 Elena: Elena, security. SOC2, KMS, and audit logs are primary for us.
00:30 Samantha: perfect. Diego will run the live sandbox demo and then we'll show the console optimize tips.

02:05 Diego: ok I'm sharing my screen. Quick note: using hosted API, streaming enabled, we'll show a chat-style generation with short system prompt. You'll see tokens stream in.
02:20 Diego: sending first request — temperature 0.2, top_p 0.9, max_tokens 120. This is what we call the low-latency profile.

03:05 (transcript glitch) Speaker 1: ...and it's, um, it starts sending partial frames, so you can render progressively, reduce perceived latency.
03:20 Diego: right, and if you look at the network trace, the initial response arrives at ~120ms on this small prompt — obviously varies by region and model.
03:40 Priya: what model is that? How different is performance between gu-2 and the quantized variants?
03:49 Diego: great question. For the demo I'm using redwood/gpt-3-like-2 (demo-tag). In prod we advise using the verified perf profile in the catalog — quantized variants drop latency a bit but sometimes increase variability. There's a trade-off — quantization can save ~30-40% token cost but may add ~20ms of per-token jitter depending on the kernel selection.
04:15 Marcus: is that kernel selection automatic?
04:20 Diego: yes the runtime picks kernels based on sequence length and hardware; customers can pin a quant profile if they want deterministic behavior.

05:02 Diego: switching to an example showing streaming interruptions — I'm going to simulate a transient error on the server side to show retry behavior.
05:18 (phone rings faintly)
05:25 Diego: ok simulated transient 502; client gets aborted stream — Redwood client SDK exposes retry plumbing. You can do two patterns: optimistic resume (KV cache resume) or safe restart (idempotent replay).
05:45 Samantha: Diego can you explain KV resume — sometimes customers hear K-V cash during calls so I always clarify.
05:52 Diego: yes — KV cache resume is where the server/client keep the KV cache for the decoder so you can resume mid-generation rather than restarting from scratch. That reduces tokens re-generated and improves perceived latency. It requires sticky routing or a short lived resume token.
06:20 Priya: does resume leak state? Any PII?
06:25 Elena: and is it compatible with our policy that no raw transcripts persist beyond 24 hours?
06:31 Diego: good callouts. Resume keys are ephemeral; you can configure cache TTLs or disable KV caching if you need strict non-persistence. For data retention, hosted logs can be turned off or configured for redaction. We integrate with customer KMS for envelope encryption in Private deployments; hosted customers can use Redwood-managed keys or bring-your-own-key in Dedicated/Private.
07:00 Priya: okay. What about idempotency tokens for safe replay?
07:05 Diego: we recommend an idempotency key per user-turn; if a request fails you can resend with the same key and the server will attempt to deduplicate. For longer-running generations we combine that with server-side resume where supported.

08:10 Marcus: how do retries interact with cost — if we try 3 times will we be billed for all tokens?
08:18 Samantha: short answer yes for raw tokens generated, but with caching/resume the incremental re-gen cost is much lower. Also Redwood Optimize can recommend batching and cache settings to lower unit cost.
08:35 Priya: can you show the console Optimize suggestion?
08:40 Diego: sure — switching to console. Under Optimize -> Model Recommendations you'll see a suggestion for our traffic pattern: use continuous batching of 50ms window and enable prefix cache for repeated system prompts. The console shows estimated token-cost delta — in our example it forecasts 18% reduction.
09:10 Ryan: is that forecast historical or simulated?
09:15 Diego: it's simulated based on request traces you upload or estimated from sample traffic; accuracy improves if you provide real traces.

10:02 Samantha: we briefly want to surface common failure modes and mitigations. Diego?
10:08 Diego: 1) transient infra errors — use exponential backoff with jitter, keep idempotency keys, and if you need low-latency fallback route to a smaller model variant. 2) partial stream with socket close — attempt resume if available, otherwise re-run with same idempotency key. 3) overloaded burst — we recommend client-side throttling + server-side autoscale on Dedicated.
10:45 Marcus: for fallback routing, is that out-of-the-box?
10:49 Diego: yes, Redwood runtime supports policy-based routing: e.g., prefer hosted gu-2, fallback to gu-2-mini on latency or cost triggers. You can configure thresholds or use the default graceful fallback.

12:00 Elena: security question — how granular are audit logs? We need per-request tracing to satisfy audit.
12:08 Samantha: Redwood provides per-request tracing IDs, token counts, latency, and model versions. For Dedicated/Private you can retain full logs in your VPC or S3 bucket under your KMS.
12:25 Elena: and SSO? We use Okta.
12:29 Samantha: we support SAML/SSO, SCIM for user sync, and RBAC roles in the console.

13:20 Diego: quick demo of retry config in SDK: show client.retry = { maxAttempts: 3, baseDelayMs: 200, maxDelayMs: 2000 } and then streaming handler with onPartialToken(...) so UI can render token-by-token.
13:45 Diego: note that for idempotency you also set client.idempotencyKey = userTurnId. Example in the repo I'll share.

15:05 Priya: what's best practice for message formatting to avoid hallucination?
15:12 Diego: structure system + user messages, provide clear instructions, and use low temperature for factual tasks. Also use reranking for top-1 reliability if you have multiple candidates. Redwood has a rerank endpoint and also supports function-calling style structured outputs to reduce free-form hallucination.

16:30 Marcus: any gotchas in large context windows? We have long conversation histories.
16:36 Diego: streaming with large context can increase latency, and KV cache helps — but you should snapshot and trim conversation context. Also consider embeddings + retrieval for long-term memory instead of sending whole history every time.

18:05 Samantha: quick pricing note for the pilot: we can set a capped pilot with quota and provide an internal cost dashboard so you won't exceed the spend.
18:20 Priya: good. What's the typical pilot length?
18:24 Samantha: usually 4 weeks — enough time to run the benchmark and production-like traffic.

19:40 Diego: I'm going to run a slightly heavier loop — 50 concurrent short chat requests to show service behavior under load.
19:55 (background typing)
20:30 Diego: you can see the console traces: latency P50 ~ 160ms, P95 ~ 420ms, and we have a few throttles showing because I used a small sandbox pool deliberately.
21:05 Priya: if we move to Dedicated, do we get SLA?
21:09 Samantha: Dedicated comes with latency and uptime SLOs plus reserved capacity. We'll map your expected QPS to a pool size and give a cost estimate.
21:25 Marcus: will we need a long procurement lead time for Dedicated?
21:28 Samantha: generally 2-4 weeks depending on region and hardware. For faster onramp we recommend starting hosted pilot and then transition to Dedicated if volume justifies it.

22:10 Elena: regulatory note: we may require on-premise for some product flows — is Private deployment full on-prem available?
22:18 Diego: yes we offer Private with customer-managed control plane and optional air-gapped install, integrates with your KMS/HSM. There are a few installation steps and security review but it's supported.

23:40 Ryan: any integration examples for message queues?
23:45 Diego: we show examples integrating with Kafka and SQS; typical pattern is to produce a request, call Redwood, and push generated response to a results topic. For idempotency you persist the idempotency key + request hash.

25:00 Priya: timeline — if we accept pilot, what's next?
25:05 Samantha: quick checklist: sign SOW, get sandbox API keys, run benchmark (Diego provides script), weekly syncs with CSM/SE. We'll set 4-week pilot.

27:10 (slight crosstalk)
27:16 Marcus: do you support token-level cost breakdown per route?
27:20 Samantha: yes console gives token-level cost and you can map cost to API key or route.

29:00 Diego: small demo showing failed stream resume: I disabled resume and retried; you'll see full re-gen billed — this shows value of KV resume.
29:25 Priya: ok good to see the delta.

31:00 Samantha: recap — key takeaways: streaming gives low perceived latency, use KV resume + idempotency keys to limit re-gen cost, enable Optimize suggestions for batching/prefix cache.
31:20 Samantha: security — Redwood supports SAML, RBAC, audit logs, and KMS integration; for strict retention you can disable hosted logs or choose Private.
31:40 Samantha: pilot — Redwood will send SOW with capped spend and Diego will share sandbox repo + benchmark.

33:05 Elena: can you include a short runbook for network egress and IP allowlist?
33:12 Diego: yes we'll include an allowlist and recommended NAT config; for Private we can detail internal network layout.

34:30 Priya: any competitors we should be mindful of when evaluating?
34:36 Samantha: customers often evaluate OpenAI for model quality and Anthropic for safety tooling; Vertex if they're deep into Google Cloud. We'll include a short comparison doc.

36:00 Ryan: one last technical — how do you handle prompt injection or malicious system messages?
36:05 Diego: we recommend prompt templates with strict system instructions, use function-calling to restrict output shapes, and for higher assurance you can run detectors or a secondary verifier model. We also have content filters at the edge.

38:20 Samantha: ok next steps again: SOW and pricing by 12/12, sandbox + bench script by 12/15, security docs to Elena by 12/13. Pilot kickoff week of 12/22.

40:10 Priya: thanks — this was very helpful.
40:14 Marcus: thanks.
40:16 Elena: appreciate it.
40:18 Samantha: thanks everyone we'll follow up in email with the artifacts. Bye.

(End of meeting)
